assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clean experimental discovery with a precise theoretical prediction behind it: at a specific small twist angle the moire flat bands produce correlated insulating and superconducting states in a tunable two-dimensional material. It opened a new platform for quantum materials, with very wide follow-on impact, and fits the discovery-or-invention criterion well. Imaging and spectroscopy of moire structure (TEM, STM) have also been central to establishing the twist-angle physics.
assessment.attribution: Theory (Bistritzer and MacDonald, flat-band magic-angle prediction) preceded the 2018 experiments (Jarillo-Herrero group), so a theory-plus-experiment configuration is natural. The experimental first author(s) are not on the credited list, and the credited strings do not cover the whole experimental team, which makes a three-person selection a judgment call.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups across several moire systems since 2018; the interpretation of the superconducting mechanism is still unsettled, but the discovery of the flat-band correlated phases is stable. Timing is reasonable though the field is still moving.
uncertainties: Credit among the experimental team and the theory pioneers (including pre-2018 moire band-structure work) may be contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Engineered subwavelength structures that give effective electromagnetic properties not found in nature (negative index, perfect-lens concept, cloaking, later metasurfaces) are a genuine invention-type advance with lasting impact on optics and photonics. The conceptual originality is high, and the experimental realisation was decisive.
assessment.attribution: Pendry supplied the key theoretical constructs (wire and split-ring-resonator media, perfect lens) and Smith led the first microwave demonstration of negative index. Capasso's contribution is chiefly to metasurfaces and generalised refraction, a later and distinct strand; so the clean pair is Pendry and Smith. Earlier work by Veselago, and parallel experimental contributions, complicate the picture.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently from microwave to optical frequencies and now in commercial and applied devices, although some early promises (optical cloaking, superlensing) have been limited by losses. Recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the negative-index and perfect-lens narrative is regarded as a physics discovery or a materials-engineering invention.
Credit relative to Veselago and other experimental groups.
Practical limits from loss and fabrication.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a textbook case of an invention based on band-structure engineering: intersubband transitions in designed heterostructures give a laser whose wavelength is set by layer thickness rather than the bandgap. It is a materials-and-growth achievement (MBE with atomic-scale layer control, verified by electron microscopy and spectroscopy) that created the mid-infrared and terahertz semiconductor laser field and has wide practical use in sensing.
assessment.attribution: The 1994 demonstration at Bell Labs was a team effort led by Faist and Capasso, with Cho's molecular-beam epitaxy growth crucial. Kazarinov and Suris proposed intersubband amplification in 1971, which is an earlier conceptual precedent that the committee would have to weigh, and other Bell Labs co-authors exist.
assessment.maturity: Over three decades of independent confirmation, commercial products and high-power room-temperature continuous-wave operation make this a mature and stable achievement; recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Prior theoretical proposal (Kazarinov and Suris) and the other original Bell Labs authors complicate attribution.
Whether the committee views the laser as sufficiently physics-driven rather than device engineering.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, established a new classification of electronic phases with robust edge and surface states. Impact on condensed matter physics and materials is very large and durable.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical step; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state (following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction). The credited list omits Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D-TI experimentalists, so the proposed trio is defensible but leaves unresolved allocation.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by many groups and by ARPES, transport and STM work on 3D topological insulators. Recognition is timely; the 2016 prize recognised related topological phase theory but not this discovery.
uncertainties: Credit allocation with Zhang (deceased), Bernevig, Hughes and three-dimensional topological insulator experimentalists.
Overlap with the 2016 prize topic may affect committee appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and in particular coherent spin-dependent tunnelling through crystalline MgO, underpins magnetic read heads and MRAM. The step from small effects to large, usable ones depended on interface and crystal-structure control that is verified by cross-sectional electron microscopy, which I know well. The topic builds on the GMR prize of 2007 and has clear technological impact.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki (large room-temperature TMR in amorphous barriers), Parkin and Yuasa (MgO(001) tunnel barriers, 2004) are the decisive experimentalists; Butler's theory of coherent tunnelling is also essential. Moodera, not on the credited list, also reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995, which makes the string list an incomplete picture of credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature, independently reproduced and industrially deployed. Timely, though the relationship to the 2007 GMR prize may reduce the perceived novelty.
uncertainties: Four credited names but a prize can name only three; Butler's theoretical role versus experimental credit is a hard choice.
Moodera's role in the 1995 discovery is outside the supplied credit.
Possible view that this is a continuation of GMR.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock idea removes motional and light-shift errors and permits fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, a major advance in precision measurement with implications for redefining the second, geodesy and tests of fundamental constants.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realised it with strontium; Ye's group advanced the stability and accuracy to the leading levels. The two-person grouping is clear, though other contributors (including ion-clock groups) share the field.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many laboratories internationally; the redefinition of the second has not yet been adopted, so the full impact is still pending, but the underlying discovery is well established.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 prize area and with trapped-ion clock developments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus tuning-fork force sensor, and CO-terminated tips enabling submolecular imaging of chemical bonds, brought non-contact AFM to routine atomic and bond-resolved imaging. This is a true instrumental invention that changed what can be seen on surfaces, in the lineage of scanning probe microscopy, and I read it as a technique with clear lasting value.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor; Gross and Meyer (IBM Zurich) made the bond-resolved imaging demonstration with functionalised tips. The partition between sensor invention and the imaging demonstration is reasonably natural for three names, though other groups contributed to atomic-resolution NC-AFM (for example earlier work in the 1990s).
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced and adopted, but its impact is concentrated in surface science and molecular imaging, so the committee may consider the breadth of physics impact less than for other candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the breadth of impact across physics is sufficient.
Earlier non-contact AFM atomic resolution work by others is outside the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices gave controllable quantum simulators of Hubbard-type models, with the observation of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and later site-resolved quantum gas microscopes. Impact on many-body physics is large and original, and it forms a cross-cutting platform.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and Cirac) proposed the lattice Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition experiment and microscope work. Credited names are four; I prefer Zoller for theory and Bloch and Greiner for experiment, but Cirac's contribution and the role of Hansch, Jaksch and others make allocation uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced by many groups; some of the promise of solving open problems (for example high-temperature superconductivity models) remains unfulfilled, so the practical-discovery framing is still developing.
uncertainties: Allocation among four credited names, plus uncredited Jaksch and Hansch contributions.
Overlap with prior prizes in cold atoms (2001, 2012, 2018).
